title: Online Evaluation: A/B Tests, Significance, Drift & Upgrade Risk
scopeHtml: Scope: Measuring real-world performance, comparing versions, statistical significance, evaluation drift and model-upgrade regressions.

notes.title: What online evaluation is and why offline is not enough
notes.html:
Online evaluation means measuring how your LLM feature performs on real users and real traffic, after (or while) it is released. Offline evaluation means running a fixed test set before release. If you have not read it yet, C7 notes 01_M1 cover datasets, graders and judges; this note starts where they stop: production.

Why offline is not enough, in plain words:

  • Your test set is a guess about what users will ask. Real users ask stranger, longer, messier, multilingual things.
  • The world moves: new products, new slang, new documents in your retrieval index. A frozen test set cannot notice.
  • Offline graders measure "is the answer correct", but the business cares about "did the customer solve their problem and not call support".
  • Models are non-deterministic. A single offline run is one sample of a random process.

So the usual lifecycle is a funnel, cheap and safe first, expensive and real last:

offline eval (fixed set, CI)        -> catches obvious breakage, free of user risk
   |
shadow mode (live traffic, hidden)  -> new version runs, nobody sees its output
   |
canary (1-5% of users)              -> real exposure, small blast radius
   |
A/B test (50/50 or similar)         -> statistical comparison on real metrics
   |
full rollout + continuous monitoring -> drift detection, sampled grading

What you measure online falls into three buckets. Keep them separate, because mixing them is the source of most bad launch decisions:

  1. Success metrics (the thing you want to improve): task completion, resolution rate, answer accepted, code suggestion kept, conversion.
  2. Guardrail metrics (things that must not get worse): latency p95, cost per request, refusal rate, safety-violation rate, error rate, escalation to human.
  3. Diagnostic metrics (to explain why): retrieval hit rate, tool-call failure rate, average output length, regeneration rate.

Real products do this constantly. GitHub Copilot-style tools track whether a suggestion was accepted and how much of it survived editing. Chat products track thumbs up/down and "regenerate" clicks. Support bots track resolution without human handoff. Search-style products track click-through and reformulation. (Exact internal metrics are not public; treat these as the commonly described patterns.)

Real life. A restaurant tests a new recipe in the kitchen first (offline), then gives free samples to a few tables (canary), then runs the new menu on half the tables and compares tips and leftovers (A/B test).

Common interview traps.

  • "We have a great offline score, so we can ship" is not enough; offline and online metrics can disagree, and online wins.
  • Guardrail metrics are not optional; a variant that improves success but doubles cost or latency may still be a loss.
  • Do not confuse online evaluation (judging live outputs) with online learning (the model updating itself); the first is just measurement.

notes.title: Instrumentation: what to log so you can evaluate later
notes.html:
You cannot evaluate what you did not record. Before any A/B test, make sure every request produces a trace: a structured record of everything that happened for that request.

Minimum fields:

  • request_id, user_id (or a hashed pseudonym), session_id, timestamp.
  • Variant info: experiment name, variant name, prompt version, model id and exact model version string returned by the provider, retrieval config version.
  • Inputs: user message, retrieved chunks (ids, scores), tool calls and results.
  • Outputs: final text, token counts (input, output, cached), finish reason, latency (time to first token and total), cost.
  • Outcomes that arrive later: thumbs, edits, copy, escalation, purchase. These arrive minutes or days later and must be joined by request_id.
user request
   |
   v
[ assign variant ] --> [ retrieve ] --> [ LLM call ] --> [ tools ] --> response
   |                      |                |              |            |
   +------ all of these write spans to one trace keyed by request_id ---+
                                   |
                                   v
                       trace store (OpenTelemetry-style)
                                   |
                       later: join with feedback events

Tools that exist for this (names only; features change, verify): Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Braintrust, Helicone, OpenTelemetry with GenAI semantic conventions, and plain data warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake) for the join with business events.

Two rules people forget:

  • Log the model version the provider actually served, not only the alias you requested. Aliases like "latest" can silently move; this is the root of many upgrade-risk incidents (see the upgrade sections).
  • Privacy: traces contain user text. Apply PII redaction, retention limits, and access control before you log, not after. See C7 02_S1 for PII handling.

A minimal trace record in three languages (a plain data holder; real systems use an SDK):

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
import time, uuid

@dataclass
class Trace:
    user_id: str
    variant: str            # "control" or "treatment"
    prompt_version: str
    model_served: str       # from the provider response, not the alias you asked for
    input_tokens: int = 0
    output_tokens: int = 0
    latency_ms: float = 0.0
    request_id: str = field(default_factory=lambda: str(uuid.uuid4()))
    ts: float = field(default_factory=time.time)
    feedback: dict = field(default_factory=dict)   # filled in later by request_id

# prints the record you would write to your log pipeline
print(Trace("u1", "treatment", "v7", "model-x-2026-01"))
import java.util.UUID

data class Trace(
    val userId: String,
    val variant: String,          // "control" or "treatment"
    val promptVersion: String,
    val modelServed: String,      // from the provider response, not the alias requested
    val inputTokens: Int = 0,
    val outputTokens: Int = 0,
    val latencyMs: Double = 0.0,
    val requestId: String = UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
    val ts: Long = System.currentTimeMillis(),
    val feedback: MutableMap<String, Any> = mutableMapOf() // joined later by requestId
)

fun main() = println(Trace("u1", "treatment", "v7", "model-x-2026-01"))
import java.util.*;

public record Trace(String userId, String variant, String promptVersion,
                    String modelServed, int inputTokens, int outputTokens,
                    double latencyMs, String requestId, long ts,
                    Map<String, Object> feedback) {
    // requestId is the join key for feedback that arrives later
    public static Trace of(String user, String variant, String prompt, String model) {
        return new Trace(user, variant, prompt, model, 0, 0, 0.0,
                UUID.randomUUID().toString(), System.currentTimeMillis(),
                new HashMap<>());
    }
}

Real life. A flight data recorder: nobody plans to crash, but when something goes wrong you need the record of exactly what happened.

Common interview traps.

  • Logging only the final answer; you also need retrieved context, prompt version and model version to diagnose a regression.
  • Forgetting that feedback arrives late; the join key and a "feedback window" (for example, wait 7 days) must be designed up front.
  • Logging raw PII "for evaluation" without redaction or retention rules.

notes.title: Online signals: implicit, explicit and automatic grading
notes.html:
Users rarely tell you the answer was wrong. You collect three kinds of signals.

Explicit feedback: thumbs up/down, star ratings, free-text comments. Pros: clear intent. Cons: very low response rate (often a few percent or less; verify for your product) and selection bias: people who bother are the delighted or the furious, not the average user.

Implicit feedback: behaviour you can observe without asking.

  • Positive: the answer was copied, the code suggestion was accepted, the user moved on to the next task, the ticket was closed without a human.
  • Negative: regenerate clicked, same question rephrased within seconds, user abandoned the session, escalated to human, heavy edits to the output.
  • Danger: implicit signals are ambiguous. A short session can mean "got the answer fast" or "gave up". Always validate a signal against human labels before trusting it.

Automatic grading on sampled traffic: run an LLM judge (or code checks) over a sample of production traces. You cannot grade 100 percent because of cost, so you sample, ideally stratified by slice (language, intent, user tier) so rare but important slices are not missed.

production traces (100%)
   |
   +--> cheap code checks on 100% (valid JSON? contains citation? length sane? refusal?)
   |
   +--> sample 1-5% (stratified) --> LLM judge (rubric) --> score store
   |
   +--> sample 0.1% + all flagged --> human review queue --> gold labels
                                           |
                                           +--> recalibrate judge, grow offline set

The last arrow is the closed loop: production failures become offline test cases. That is how the offline set stays alive.

Judge-on-sample in python (the SDK shapes are standard; model id is an example, verify before use). Kotlin and Java would use the Anthropic Java SDK or plain HTTP in the same way, so only the Python version is shown here to avoid repeating boilerplate; the sampling decision itself is shown in three languages in the next section.

import json, anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

RUBRIC = """Score the ANSWER to the QUESTION from 1 to 5 for factual correctness
given the CONTEXT only. Reply with JSON: {"score": int, "reason": str}."""

def judge(question: str, context: str, answer: str) -> dict:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-5-5",       # example id; verify against docs
        max_tokens=200,
        system=RUBRIC,
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"QUESTION: {question}\nCONTEXT: {context}\nANSWER: {answer}"}],
    )
    return json.loads(msg.content[0].text)   # production code must handle bad JSON

# returns e.g. {"score": 4, "reason": "..."}

Pitfalls of online judging: judge cost grows with traffic; the judge drifts too (provider changes it), so re-check it against a small frozen set of human-labelled examples every so often. Use a different model family or at least a different model than the one being judged to reduce self-preference bias (see 01_M1).

Real life. A hotel: comment cards (explicit, few and biased), watching whether guests re-book (implicit), and a mystery shopper who inspects a sample of rooms (sampled grading).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating thumbs-down rate as a precise quality number; response rates are tiny and biased.
  • Using regenerate or session length as a quality metric without validating against labels.
  • Sampling uniformly and missing a rare but critical slice (for example, a minority language).

notes.title: Shadow mode, canary and gradual rollout
notes.html:
Before you A/B test with real exposure, there are safer stages.

Shadow mode (also called dark launch): the new version receives a copy of live requests and produces outputs, but users only see the old version's output. You then compare outputs and metrics offline.

  • Good for: checking cost, latency, error rates, format failures, and comparing outputs with a judge, with zero user risk.
  • Limits: you do not get user behaviour (users never saw it), and for agents with side effects (sending email, writing to a database) shadow runs must use stubbed or read-only tools. Shadow also doubles your inference bill for the shadowed share.

Canary release: the new version serves a small slice (1 to 5 percent) of real users. Watch guardrail metrics for a fixed period; roll back automatically if they breach thresholds. A canary is primarily a safety check, not a proof of improvement: a slice that small rarely has enough data to prove a quality win (see sample size, below).

Gradual rollout (ramp): 1% to 5% to 25% to 50% to 100%, with a gate between each step.

stage      traffic   purpose                     auto-rollback if
shadow     0% seen   cost/latency/format check   error rate > baseline + X
canary     1-5%      guardrails on real users    safety violations up, p95 latency +20%
A/B        10-50%    prove quality win           guardrail breach OR stat. significant loss
ramp       100%      done; keep a holdout        drift alarm

A holdout (a small permanent control group, say 1 to 5 percent kept on the old version, or on no-AI behaviour) lets you keep measuring long-term effects and drift, instead of only comparing against your memory of how things used to be.

Sticky assignment matters: a user must see the same variant on every request, otherwise a conversation switches personality midway and your data is contaminated. The standard trick is deterministic hashing of the user id with the experiment name:

import hashlib

def bucket(user_id: str, experiment: str, treatment_pct: float) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256(f"{experiment}:{user_id}".encode()).hexdigest()
    slot = int(h[:8], 16) % 10_000          # 0..9999, stable for this user+experiment
    return "treatment" if slot < treatment_pct * 100 else "control"

# same user always gets the same answer; prints "control" or "treatment"
print(bucket("user-42", "prompt-v7", 10.0))
import java.security.MessageDigest

fun bucket(userId: String, experiment: String, treatmentPct: Double): String {
    val digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
        .digest("$experiment:$userId".toByteArray())
    // first 4 bytes as an unsigned int, like int(h[:8], 16) in the Python version
    val n = ((digest[0].toLong() and 0xff) shl 24) or ((digest[1].toLong() and 0xff) shl 16) or
            ((digest[2].toLong() and 0xff) shl 8) or (digest[3].toLong() and 0xff)
    val slot = (n % 10_000).toInt()
    return if (slot < treatmentPct * 100) "treatment" else "control"
}

fun main() = println(bucket("user-42", "prompt-v7", 10.0))
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class Bucketing {
    static String bucket(String userId, String experiment, double treatmentPct) throws Exception {
        byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
            .digest((experiment + ":" + userId).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        long n = ((d[0] & 0xffL) << 24) | ((d[1] & 0xffL) << 16) | ((d[2] & 0xffL) << 8) | (d[3] & 0xffL);
        int slot = (int) (n % 10_000);
        return slot < treatmentPct * 100 ? "treatment" : "control";
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
        System.out.println(bucket("user-42", "prompt-v7", 10.0)); // stable per user
    }
}

Why include the experiment name in the hash? Otherwise the same users would always land in treatment for every experiment, and effects from different experiments would be correlated. Also, increasing the percentage (10 to 25) keeps existing treatment users in treatment, because their slot number does not change.

Real life. Opening a new restaurant branch: a soft launch for friends and family (shadow), then limited hours (canary), then the grand opening (ramp), while the old branch stays open as a comparison (holdout).

Common interview traps.

  • Randomizing per request instead of per user; users then see inconsistent behaviour and the samples are not independent.
  • Running shadow mode with real side-effecting tools.
  • Calling a 2% canary "an A/B test"; it has far too little data to detect small quality differences.

notes.title: A/B testing prompts and models step by step
notes.html:
An A/B test compares two versions (A = control, B = treatment) by randomly assigning users to each and comparing a metric. Random assignment is what makes it causal: any difference beyond noise must be due to the change, because everything else (time of day, user mix) is balanced by chance.

Step by step:

  1. Hypothesis: "Prompt v7 (adds step-by-step instructions) raises resolution rate."
  2. Primary metric: pick exactly one before the test. Example: resolution rate without human handoff.
  3. Guardrails: p95 latency, cost per resolved ticket, safety-violation rate.
  4. Unit of randomization: usually the user (not the request, not the session, unless the product is truly one-shot).
  5. Sample size and duration: compute before starting (next sections). Include at least one full weekly cycle, because Monday users differ from Saturday users.
  6. Run without peeking and deciding early (peeking rules below).
  7. Check data quality first: the sample ratio must match your intended split. If you planned 50/50 and see 52/48 on a million users, something is broken (this check is called sample ratio mismatch, SRM). Do not analyze a broken experiment.
  8. Analyze: effect size, confidence interval, p-value, guardrails, slices.
  9. Decide and document: ship, iterate or kill. Keep a holdout.

LLM-specific wrinkles:

  • Variance is higher than in classic UI tests: the same prompt gives different outputs, and answer quality is often judged by a noisy grader. Noisy metrics need more samples.
  • Novelty effect: users react to a changed tone for a few days. Run long enough for the effect to settle.
  • Change one thing at a time: if you change the model, the prompt and the retrieval at once, a win teaches you nothing. Use a factorial design only if you can afford the traffic.
  • Interaction with caching: a prompt change invalidates prompt caches (see C5 notes on caching if present), so treatment cost may look worse at first; measure after warm-up.
  • Multi-turn conversations: the unit is the conversation or the user, not the message; messages inside one conversation are correlated.
  • Network effects and shared memory: if variants share a knowledge base or a cache, treatment can leak into control.

Offline-to-online link: before spending traffic, require the new variant to win or tie on the offline suite. Online tests are expensive, so offline is the filter and online is the judge.

Platforms people use (verify current features): Statsig, Optimizely, LaunchDarkly experiments, GrowthBook, Eppo, or an in-house flag service plus warehouse queries. LLM-specific eval platforms (Braintrust, Langfuse, LangSmith) compare prompt variants on logged traffic too.

Real life. Two sections of one class are taught the same topic with different methods and then take the same quiz. It only works if students were assigned to sections randomly, not because the strong ones picked one.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing the success metric after seeing the results ("metric shopping").
  • Ignoring sample ratio mismatch and analyzing a broken split.
  • Randomizing per message in a chat product, which contaminates conversations.
  • Changing the prompt mid-experiment; the experiment is now about nothing in particular.

notes.title: Statistical significance from zero
notes.html:
You run an A/B test: control resolves 600 of 1,000 conversations (60.0 percent), treatment resolves 630 of 1,000 (63.0 percent). Is treatment better, or did you get lucky?

Noise first. Even if the two versions were identical, two random groups of 1,000 would not give exactly the same count. The difference you observed could be pure chance. Statistical significance is the tool for asking: "if there were truly no difference, how surprising would a gap this big be?"

Vocabulary, plainly:

  • Null hypothesis (H0): there is no real difference.
  • p-value: the probability of seeing a gap at least this large if H0 were true. A small p (conventionally below 0.05) means "this would be rare by luck alone". It is NOT the probability that treatment is better, and NOT the probability the result is a fluke.
  • Significance level (alpha): the false-alarm rate you accept, usually 0.05.
  • Confidence interval (CI): a range of plausible true differences. A 95 percent CI that excludes zero corresponds to p below 0.05 at alpha 0.05.
  • Effect size: how big the difference is (3 percentage points here). Significance says "real", effect size says "worth caring about".

Now the math for the two-proportion z-test, shown step by step with the numbers above:

p1 = 600/1000 = 0.600     p2 = 630/1000 = 0.630     difference d = 0.030
pooled p = (600+630)/(1000+1000) = 0.615
standard error SE = sqrt( p(1-p) * (1/n1 + 1/n2) )
                  = sqrt( 0.615*0.385 * (0.001 + 0.001) )
                  = sqrt( 0.236775 * 0.002 )
                  = sqrt( 0.00047355 ) = 0.02176
z = d / SE = 0.030 / 0.02176 = 1.38
two-sided critical value at alpha 0.05 = 1.96
1.38 < 1.96  => NOT significant (p is roughly 0.17)
95% CI for d = 0.030 +/- 1.96*0.02176 = 0.030 +/- 0.0427 = [-0.013, +0.073]

Read that last line carefully: the CI runs from -1.3 points (treatment slightly worse) to +7.3 points (much better). The data is simply compatible with both. The honest conclusion is "inconclusive", not "no effect" and not "B wins".

The same test in code:

import math

def two_prop_z(succ_a, n_a, succ_b, n_b):
    p_a, p_b = succ_a / n_a, succ_b / n_b
    pooled = (succ_a + succ_b) / (n_a + n_b)
    se = math.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / n_a + 1 / n_b))
    z = (p_b - p_a) / se
    # unpooled SE for the confidence interval of the difference
    se_ci = math.sqrt(p_a * (1 - p_a) / n_a + p_b * (1 - p_b) / n_b)
    d = p_b - p_a
    return z, (d - 1.96 * se_ci, d + 1.96 * se_ci)

z, ci = two_prop_z(600, 1000, 630, 1000)
print(round(z, 2), [round(x, 3) for x in ci])   # ~1.38, CI includes 0 -> inconclusive
import kotlin.math.sqrt

fun twoPropZ(sa: Int, na: Int, sb: Int, nb: Int): Pair<Double, Pair<Double, Double>> {
    val pa = sa.toDouble() / na
    val pb = sb.toDouble() / nb
    val pooled = (sa + sb).toDouble() / (na + nb)
    val se = sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1.0 / na + 1.0 / nb))
    val z = (pb - pa) / se
    val seCi = sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) / na + pb * (1 - pb) / nb)
    val d = pb - pa
    return z to ((d - 1.96 * seCi) to (d + 1.96 * seCi))
}

fun main() = println(twoPropZ(600, 1000, 630, 1000)) // z ~ 1.38, CI spans 0
public class ZTest {
    static double[] twoPropZ(int sa, int na, int sb, int nb) {
        double pa = (double) sa / na, pb = (double) sb / nb;
        double pooled = (double) (sa + sb) / (na + nb);
        double se = Math.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1.0 / na + 1.0 / nb));
        double z = (pb - pa) / se;
        double seCi = Math.sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) / na + pb * (1 - pb) / nb);
        double d = pb - pa;
        return new double[]{z, d - 1.96 * seCi, d + 1.96 * seCi};
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(twoPropZ(600, 1000, 630, 1000))); // ~1.38
    }
}

When to use something else: the z-test is for yes/no outcomes with decent counts (a rule of thumb is at least ~10 successes and failures per group). For continuous metrics (latency, cost, 1-to-5 scores) use a t-test or a bootstrap. For heavy-tailed metrics (cost, latency) use medians/percentiles with bootstrap, because one huge outlier can wreck a mean.

Real life. Flip a coin 10 times, get 6 heads. You would not accuse the coin of being biased; the p-value and CI are the formal version of that common-sense reaction.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "p = 0.05 means there is a 95 percent chance B is better"; the p-value is about the data given H0, not about the hypothesis.
  • Concluding "no effect" from a non-significant result; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, look at the CI.
  • Reporting significance without effect size; with a million users a 0.05-point change can be significant and useless.
  • Using a z-test on tiny counts or on heavy-tailed metrics.

notes.title: Sample size, power and the peeking problem
notes.html:
The test above was inconclusive partly because 1,000 per arm is too small for a 3-point effect. Power is the probability that your test detects a real effect of a given size (typical target: 80 percent). Sample size, effect size, noise and power are tied together; you pick three and the fourth follows.

Quick formula for comparing two proportions (per arm, alpha 0.05 two-sided, power 80 percent):

n per arm  ~=  2 * (z_alpha/2 + z_power)^2 * p(1-p) / d^2
z_alpha/2 = 1.96, z_power = 0.84  => (1.96+0.84)^2 = 2.8^2 = 7.84
baseline p = 0.60, minimum detectable effect d = 0.03
p(1-p) = 0.60*0.40 = 0.24
n = 2 * 7.84 * 0.24 / 0.03^2 = 3.7632 / 0.0009 = about 4,181 per arm

So about 4,200 users per arm, not 1,000. And the dependence on d is squared: to detect a 1.5-point effect (half as big), you need four times as many, roughly 16,700 per arm. This is why small canaries cannot prove small wins.

def n_per_arm(p, mde, z_alpha=1.96, z_power=0.84):
    # rough two-proportion sample size; use a stats library for production planning
    return 2 * (z_alpha + z_power) ** 2 * p * (1 - p) / mde ** 2

print(round(n_per_arm(0.60, 0.03)))   # ~4181
fun nPerArm(p: Double, mde: Double, zAlpha: Double = 1.96, zPower: Double = 0.84): Double =
    2 * Math.pow(zAlpha + zPower, 2.0) * p * (1 - p) / (mde * mde)

fun main() = println(Math.round(nPerArm(0.60, 0.03))) // ~4181
public class SampleSize {
    static double nPerArm(double p, double mde) {
        double z = 1.96 + 0.84;
        return 2 * z * z * p * (1 - p) / (mde * mde);
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(Math.round(nPerArm(0.60, 0.03))); // ~4181
    }
}

The peeking problem. If you check the p-value every day and stop the moment it dips below 0.05, your real false-positive rate is far above 5 percent, because you gave randomness many chances to look like a win. Two honest options:

  • Fixed horizon: decide the sample size in advance, look once at the end.
  • Sequential testing: use methods built for continuous monitoring (group-sequential boundaries, alpha-spending, always-valid p-values or Bayesian approaches). Many experiment platforms offer these; verify which one yours uses.

Multiple comparisons. Test 20 variants or 20 metrics at alpha 0.05 and you expect about one false win by chance (20 * 0.05 = 1). Fixes: pre-register one primary metric; apply Bonferroni (divide alpha by the number of tests, so 0.05/20 = 0.0025) or Benjamini-Hochberg (controls the false discovery rate); treat slice-level wins as hypotheses to confirm, not conclusions.

Practical significance. Decide in advance the minimum detectable effect worth shipping. If the new model costs 40 percent more, a 0.5-point gain may not justify it even if it is significant.

Real life. Judging a coin by 5 flips versus 5,000 flips; and re-checking the scoreboard every minute until your team happens to lead, then declaring victory.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting a test without computing sample size, then running until "it looks significant".
  • Forgetting that halving the detectable effect quadruples the sample.
  • Slicing results by 15 segments and announcing the one that "won".
  • Treating non-significance as a reason to extend the test indefinitely.

notes.title: Statistics that fit LLM metrics: paired tests, bootstrap, noisy graders
notes.html:
Online A/B tests compare different users in each arm. But a lot of LLM evaluation is cheaper and sharper if you can compare both versions on the same inputs.

Paired comparison. Take the same N prompts (from shadow mode or a replayed sample of production traffic), run both variants, grade both outputs. Now per-prompt differences cancel out "this question is just hard" noise. Example: 200 prompts, A wins 30, B wins 50, 120 ties. Only the 80 disagreements carry information; the sign test or McNemar's test asks whether 50 vs 30 is more lopsided than a fair coin:

disagreements n = 80, B wins k = 50
expected under H0 = 40, SD = sqrt(80 * 0.5 * 0.5) = sqrt(20) = 4.47
z = (50 - 40) / 4.47 = 2.24  (with continuity correction (49.5-40)/4.47 = 2.12)
> 1.96 => significant at 0.05 (roughly p = 0.03)

Notice the same 50 versus 30 split would be far less convincing if you had to treat the two arms as independent groups of different users. Pairing is the main reason offline replays are powerful.

Bootstrap confidence intervals. For any metric (median latency, mean judge score, F1) resample your per-item results with replacement many times, recompute the metric each time, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the CI. No formula needed.

import numpy as np

def bootstrap_diff_ci(a, b, iters=10_000, seed=0):
    # a, b: per-prompt scores for the same prompts (paired). Returns 95% CI of mean(b-a).
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    d = np.asarray(b, float) - np.asarray(a, float)
    means = [rng.choice(d, size=len(d), replace=True).mean() for _ in range(iters)]
    return np.percentile(means, [2.5, 97.5])

# if the interval excludes 0, the paired improvement is unlikely to be luck
import java.util.Random

fun bootstrapDiffCi(a: DoubleArray, b: DoubleArray, iters: Int = 10_000, seed: Long = 0): Pair<Double, Double> {
    val d = DoubleArray(a.size) { b[it] - a[it] }
    val rnd = Random(seed)
    val means = DoubleArray(iters) {
        var s = 0.0
        repeat(d.size) { s += d[rnd.nextInt(d.size)] }
        s / d.size
    }
    means.sort()
    return means[(iters * 0.025).toInt()] to means[(iters * 0.975).toInt()]
}
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Random;

public class Bootstrap {
    static double[] diffCi(double[] a, double[] b, int iters, long seed) {
        int n = a.length;
        double[] d = new double[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) d[i] = b[i] - a[i];
        Random rnd = new Random(seed);
        double[] means = new double[iters];
        for (int t = 0; t < iters; t++) {
            double s = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += d[rnd.nextInt(n)];
            means[t] = s / n;
        }
        Arrays.sort(means);
        return new double[]{means[(int) (iters * 0.025)], means[(int) (iters * 0.975)]};
    }
}

Noise sources specific to LLMs (see also 01_M1, "Metrics and statistics"):

  • Sampling noise: temperature above 0 means the same prompt gives different outputs. Run several samples per prompt, or set temperature 0 for the offline comparison and accept that production uses a different setting.
  • Judge noise and bias: an LLM judge gives slightly different scores each time and may prefer longer answers. Measure judge agreement with humans, and include it in your uncertainty (a noisy grader widens CIs).
  • Provider nondeterminism: even at temperature 0, outputs can vary between calls because of batching and hardware (commonly reported; verify for your provider). Never assume a bit-exact repeat.
  • Heavy tails: cost and latency distributions have long tails. Report p50, p95, p99, not just the mean.
  • Cluster correlation: messages from one user are not independent; analyze at the user level or use cluster-robust methods.

Variance reduction helps small teams: CUPED (adjust the metric using each user's pre-experiment behaviour as a covariate) and stratified sampling can cut the required sample noticeably. These are standard in experimentation platforms (verify support in yours).

Real life. Comparing two tutors by giving both the same exam paper rather than different students different papers: the shared paper removes "this exam was just hard" from the comparison.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating the two arms of a replay as independent when they share inputs; use a paired test.
  • Ignoring judge noise and reporting a tight CI that only reflects sampling of prompts.
  • Reporting mean latency or cost where percentiles tell the real story.
  • Assuming temperature 0 guarantees identical outputs.

notes.title: Evaluation drift: when quality changes without a code change
notes.html:
Evaluation drift here means your measured quality changes over time even though you did not deliberately change anything, or your evaluation tools themselves quietly stop measuring what you think. The word is used loosely; it helps to split it into four kinds:

  1. Input (data) drift: the user questions change. New product launches, seasonality (tax season), a new language, a viral prompt format. Your model and prompt are the same, but they now face different inputs.
  2. Concept drift: the right answer changes. Prices, policies, laws, API versions. A previously correct answer becomes stale. Retrieval-augmented systems drift when documents change or the index goes stale.
  3. Model drift (provider-side): the model behind an alias changes, gets patched, or the provider adjusts safety filters, tokenization, or serving stack. Studies of hosted LLMs have reported behaviour changing over months for the same named model (verify the specifics; the principle is the point). Pinned dated versions reduce this but do not eliminate infrastructure-level changes.
  4. Evaluator drift: your LLM judge's underlying model changes, or your rubric is applied differently, so scores shift while the product did not. Also eval-set staleness: the offline suite no longer resembles traffic, so "99 percent pass" means nothing.
what changed?      detected by                         first response
input mix          embedding / intent / length drift   refresh eval set, check slices
facts / documents  freshness checks, groundedness      re-index, expire stale chunks
provider model     canary prompts, pinned-version diff open provider ticket, pin, roll back
judge / rubric     frozen human-labelled calibration   recalibrate or replace judge

How to detect it.

  • Monitor metrics over time with control limits: judge scores on a sampled stream, refusal rate, average output length, format-failure rate, thumbs-down rate, tool error rate. Alert on moves beyond normal weekly noise, not on every wiggle. Compare the same weekday to the same weekday.
  • Input drift statistics: the Population Stability Index (PSI) compares the distribution of some feature (query length bucket, intent category, language) between a reference window and the current window. PSI = sum over buckets of (cur% - ref%) * ln(cur% / ref%). A common rule of thumb: below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate shift, above 0.25 major shift (a convention from credit-scoring practice; treat thresholds as starting points).
  • Canary prompts: a small fixed set (say 50 to 200 prompts) with known good answers, run on a schedule (for example hourly or daily) against the live provider endpoint. It is your smoke detector for provider-side changes, because the inputs never change, so any shift in output must come from the model, tools or infrastructure.
  • Frozen calibration set for the judge: human-labelled examples scored by the judge regularly; if agreement falls, the judge drifted.
  • Embedding drift: embed recent queries, compare their centroid or cluster mix with a reference window. Also watch retrieval scores: a falling average top-1 similarity often means the corpus or queries moved.

Worked PSI example with three buckets of query length (short/medium/long):

ref:  50% / 30% / 20%      cur:  30% / 30% / 40%
bucket1: (0.30-0.50) * ln(0.30/0.50) = (-0.20) * (-0.5108) = 0.1022
bucket2: (0.30-0.30) * ln(1)         = 0
bucket3: (0.40-0.20) * ln(0.40/0.20) = ( 0.20) * ( 0.6931) = 0.1386
PSI = 0.1022 + 0 + 0.1386 = 0.241  -> borderline major shift, investigate
import math

def psi(ref, cur, eps=1e-6):
    # ref, cur: lists of bucket proportions that each sum to 1
    return sum((c - r) * math.log((c + eps) / (r + eps)) for r, c in zip(ref, cur))

print(round(psi([0.5, 0.3, 0.2], [0.3, 0.3, 0.4]), 3))   # ~0.241
import kotlin.math.ln

fun psi(ref: List<Double>, cur: List<Double>, eps: Double = 1e-6): Double =
    ref.zip(cur).sumOf { (r, c) -> (c - r) * ln((c + eps) / (r + eps)) }

fun main() = println(psi(listOf(0.5, 0.3, 0.2), listOf(0.3, 0.3, 0.4))) // ~0.241
public class Psi {
    static double psi(double[] ref, double[] cur) {
        double eps = 1e-6, s = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < ref.length; i++)
            s += (cur[i] - ref[i]) * Math.log((cur[i] + eps) / (ref[i] + eps));
        return s;
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(psi(new double[]{.5, .3, .2}, new double[]{.3, .3, .4})); // ~0.241
    }
}

Production failure patterns:

  • Quality "slowly gets worse" for weeks, nobody notices because the dashboard shows only a 30-day average. Fix: compare windows and slice.
  • The knowledge base was updated but old chunks remain in the index; the bot confidently quotes last year's policy.
  • The judge model was auto-upgraded; scores jump up 0.3 points overnight and a team celebrates a quality gain that never happened.
  • A seasonal spike (holiday returns) shifts input mix, so a healthy system fails the old thresholds.

Tools: Evidently, Arize, WhyLabs-style monitors, Langfuse/LangSmith score dashboards, and plain scheduled jobs plus a warehouse (verify current products; the market changes).

Real life. A bathroom scale that slowly drifts: your weight did not change, the instrument did. Canary prompts are the known 10 kg test weight you place on it every morning.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up data drift (inputs changed) and concept drift (the correct answers changed); the fixes differ.
  • Forgetting that the evaluator can drift too; calibrate the judge continuously.
  • Alerting on a raw threshold with no seasonality baseline, causing alert fatigue.
  • Believing a pinned model version means nothing can change; infrastructure, tokenizer, safety layers or your own retrieval data still can.

notes.title: Upgrade risk: model and provider changes
notes.html:
Upgrade risk is the chance that swapping or updating the model (or the provider, SDK, parameters or surrounding stack) makes your product worse in ways the benchmark headlines do not show. A newer model usually scores better on public benchmarks, yet your prompts were tuned for the old one.

Typical ways upgrades break things:

  • Format changes: the new model wraps JSON in prose or code fences, changes list style, or adds more caveats, and your parser fails.
  • Style and verbosity: longer or shorter answers change UX, token cost and latency.
  • Instruction following shifts: a prompt hack that worked (all-caps warnings, specific phrasing) is now ignored or over-obeyed. Newer models are often more literal.
  • Refusal and safety behaviour: more or fewer refusals, different handling of borderline requests.
  • Tool-calling behaviour: different argument formats, different decisions about when to call tools, different multi-step habits in agents.
  • Tokenizer changes: different token counts change cost and may break max-token budgets and truncation assumptions.
  • Parameter changes: some model generations restrict or remove parameters (for example sampling controls) or change defaults; check the migration guide (verify in the provider docs).
  • Deprecation: providers retire model versions on published schedules. A hard-coded old id eventually returns errors; an alias silently moves you to a new model. Both are risks; the first is loud, the second is quiet.
  • Provider switch: an "OpenAI-compatible" endpoint is rarely identical in tool-calling, streaming events, JSON mode, or error codes.

The defence is a repeatable upgrade playbook:

1. Pin exact model ids (dated snapshots where offered); never "latest" in production.
2. Subscribe to deprecation notices; keep a calendar of retirement dates.
3. Keep a regression suite: critical flows, past incidents, adversarial and safety cases, per-slice.
4. Run old vs new on the suite (paired). Compare per slice, cost, latency, format-failure rate.
5. Fix prompts for the new model; re-evaluate. Do not carry old hacks blindly.
6. Shadow on live traffic; diff outputs; judge a sample.
7. Canary 1-5% with auto-rollback on guardrails; then A/B for the quality claim.
8. Ramp with a holdout; keep the old version deployable (one config flag) for at least one cycle.

A regression gate in code. The rule: fail the upgrade if any important slice drops by more than a tolerance beyond what noise can explain. This sketch uses a simple conservative test: the drop must exceed tolerance and its z-score must indicate it is not noise.

import math

def regression_gate(old, new, tolerance=0.02, z_crit=1.645):
    """old/new: {slice: (passes, total)}. Returns list of slices that regressed."""
    bad = []
    for name, (po, no) in old.items():
        pn, nn = new[name]
        p_o, p_n = po / no, pn / nn
        se = math.sqrt(p_o * (1 - p_o) / no + p_n * (1 - p_n) / nn) or 1e-9
        drop = p_o - p_n
        if drop > tolerance and drop / se > z_crit:   # real AND bigger than we accept
            bad.append((name, round(drop, 3)))
    return bad

old = {"billing": (460, 500), "refunds": (270, 300)}
new = {"billing": (430, 500), "refunds": (268, 300)}
print(regression_gate(old, new))   # [('billing', 0.06)] -> block the upgrade
import kotlin.math.sqrt

data class Counts(val pass: Int, val total: Int)

fun regressionGate(
    old: Map<String, Counts>, new: Map<String, Counts>,
    tolerance: Double = 0.02, zCrit: Double = 1.645
): List<Pair<String, Double>> = old.mapNotNull { (name, o) ->
    val n = new.getValue(name)
    val po = o.pass.toDouble() / o.total
    val pn = n.pass.toDouble() / n.total
    val se = sqrt(po * (1 - po) / o.total + pn * (1 - pn) / n.total).takeIf { it > 0 } ?: 1e-9
    val drop = po - pn
    if (drop > tolerance && drop / se > zCrit) name to drop else null
}

fun main() {
    val old = mapOf("billing" to Counts(460, 500), "refunds" to Counts(270, 300))
    val new = mapOf("billing" to Counts(430, 500), "refunds" to Counts(268, 300))
    println(regressionGate(old, new)) // billing regressed by ~0.06
}
import java.util.*;

public class RegressionGate {
    record Counts(int pass, int total) {}

    static List<String> gate(Map<String, Counts> oldM, Map<String, Counts> newM,
                             double tolerance, double zCrit) {
        List<String> bad = new ArrayList<>();
        for (var e : oldM.entrySet()) {
            Counts o = e.getValue(), n = newM.get(e.getKey());
            double po = (double) o.pass() / o.total(), pn = (double) n.pass() / n.total();
            double se = Math.sqrt(po * (1 - po) / o.total() + pn * (1 - pn) / n.total());
            if (se == 0) se = 1e-9;
            double drop = po - pn;
            if (drop > tolerance && drop / se > zCrit) bad.add(e.getKey() + " -" + drop);
        }
        return bad;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var o = Map.of("billing", new Counts(460, 500), "refunds", new Counts(270, 300));
        var n = Map.of("billing", new Counts(430, 500), "refunds", new Counts(268, 300));
        System.out.println(gate(o, n, 0.02, 1.645)); // [billing -0.06...]
    }
}

Check of the Python numbers: billing old 460/500 = 0.92, new 430/500 = 0.86, drop 0.06; SE = sqrt(0.920.08/500 + 0.860.14/500) = sqrt(0.0001472 + 0.0002408) = sqrt(0.000388) = 0.01970; z = 0.06/0.0197 = 3.05 > 1.645 and drop above 0.02, so it is flagged. Refunds: 0.9 vs 0.8933, drop 0.0067, below tolerance, passes.

Note this runs one test per slice, so with many slices raise z_crit (multiple comparisons) or accept a few false alarms for safety slices, where a false alarm is cheap and a miss is costly. Asymmetric thresholds for safety-critical slices are a legitimate design choice.

Real incident patterns: a JSON-extraction pipeline fails 8 percent of calls after an upgrade because the model now adds a leading sentence; a customer-support bot's average answer length doubles, raising cost and truncating on mobile; a deprecated model id is retired and every request returns an error on the retirement day nobody tracked; an alias moves to a new model overnight and refund-policy answers subtly change.

Real life. Replacing the engine of a delivery van with a newer, more powerful one: you still test the brakes, the cargo door and the fuel gauge before putting it on the road, and you keep the old van parked in case.

Common interview traps.

  • Trusting public benchmark gains; they say little about your prompts, data and format requirements.
  • Using a floating alias like "latest" in production.
  • Evaluating only the average; the regression hides in one slice or in the tail.
  • Forgetting non-quality changes: token counts, latency, rate limits, parameter support.
  • No rollback path; a model swap should be a config change, not a deploy.

notes.title: Putting it together: a release decision playbook
notes.html:
Here is how a mature team ties everything into one repeatable decision, using a concrete scenario.

Scenario. A support assistant answers billing questions with prompt v6 on model M1. The team wants prompt v7 on newer model M2 (cheaper, faster, higher public benchmarks). Baseline resolution rate: 60 percent. They care about improvements of 3 points or more.

  1. Offline gate (hours): run the regression suite, paired old vs new. Require no slice regression beyond tolerance, format-failure rate not worse, safety suite clean. Result: pass, but the "refunds" slice shows a slightly different tone, noted for review.
  2. Prompt adaptation: M2 follows instructions more literally; shorten the prompt, remove shouting, re-run offline.
  3. Shadow (days): replay 1 week of live traffic, 20k requests. Cost per request down 25 percent (check: if M1 was 4 cents and M2 3 cents, then (4-3)/4 = 25 percent; verify with real pricing). p95 latency better. Judge sample shows parity, 40 disagreement cases hand-read.
  4. Canary (2 days, 2 percent): guardrails only. No safety increase, no latency regressions, error rate flat.
  5. A/B (sized beforehand): to detect a 3-point lift at baseline 60 percent needs about 4,181 users per arm (see the sample-size math), so the plan is roughly 4,200 per arm plus a safety margin for dropouts and a minimum of 14 days to cover weekday cycles. Primary metric: resolution without handoff. One look at the end (or a sequential method).
  6. Decide with a table:
metric                  control   treatment   diff     95% CI           verdict
resolution rate         60.1%     61.6%       +1.5     [-0.4, +3.4]     inconclusive on quality
cost per conversation   $0.040    $0.030      -25%     [-27%, -23%]     clear win
p95 latency             6.2 s     4.9 s       -1.3 s   [-1.6, -1.0]     clear win
safety violations       0.10%     0.11%       +0.01    [-0.04, +0.06]   no evidence of harm

(numbers illustrative.) Here quality did not clearly improve, but it did not clearly drop either, and cost and latency improved. A reasonable decision is "ship as a cost win", stating plainly that no quality lift was proven. That is an honest, defensible outcome; forcing a quality narrative is not. 7. Ramp with a holdout (5 percent stay on the old setup for a month); keep the canary prompts and drift monitors running; schedule a judge-calibration check. 8. Close the loop: every bad production example found goes into the offline set with a label.

Organizational habits that matter as much as the math:

  • Write the decision rule before seeing results.
  • Maintain a changelog: prompt version, model id, retrieval config, judge version, with dates, so drift can be correlated with changes.
  • Own an on-call runbook: who can roll back, what the alert thresholds are, where the old config lives.
  • Review a handful of raw outputs weekly; metrics never replace reading examples.

Android and mobile note: if the client is an Android app, keep the experiment assignment and the model call on your backend (never ship API keys in the app). The app should only send the user id and receive the response. Client-side feature flags (Firebase Remote Config and similar) can pass the variant label for UI differences, but the LLM variant decision belongs server-side so the trace is complete. On-device models (for example Gemini Nano via ML Kit GenAI) change with OS and Play services updates outside your release cycle, which is itself an upgrade-risk source; log the on-device model version and sample outputs where privacy allows (verify current APIs).

Real life. A pilot's pre-flight checklist: each item is dull, none is optional, and the sequence exists because skipping one has historically caused crashes.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping straight to an A/B test without an offline gate or shadow stage.
  • Declaring victory on cost or latency and quietly implying a quality gain.
  • Skipping the holdout, so months later nobody can tell whether the system is improving or decaying.
  • Letting the client decide the LLM variant, which leaks keys and breaks traces.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Online evaluation. Offline tests are necessary but not sufficient: real inputs, real behaviour and shifting data need live measurement. Use a funnel: offline, shadow, canary, A/B, ramp with a holdout. Track success metrics, guardrail metrics and diagnostic metrics separately.

Instrumentation. Log request id, variant, prompt version, the model version actually served, retrieval context, tokens, latency, cost and later feedback. Redact PII. You cannot evaluate what you did not record.

Signals. Explicit feedback is clear but sparse and biased; implicit feedback is plentiful but ambiguous and needs validation; sampled automatic grading scales quality checks but costs money and has its own bias. Close the loop by turning production failures into offline cases.

A/B testing. Randomize per user with sticky deterministic hashing, choose one primary metric and guardrails in advance, check sample ratio mismatch, run whole weekly cycles, and change one thing at a time.

Significance. The p-value measures surprise under "no difference", not the chance B is better. Read the confidence interval and effect size; a non-significant result with a wide CI is inconclusive, not "no effect". Worked example: 60 percent vs 63 percent with 1,000 per arm gives z about 1.38, CI roughly -1.3 to +7.3 points, inconclusive.

Power and pitfalls. Sample size per arm is about 2 (1.96+0.84)^2 p(1-p) / d^2, about 4,181 for p = 0.6 and d = 0.03; halving d quadruples it. Avoid peeking (or use sequential methods), correct for multiple comparisons, and require practical significance.

LLM-specific statistics. Use paired tests and bootstrap CIs on replayed inputs, account for sampling, judge and provider noise, report percentiles for heavy-tailed metrics, and analyze at the user level.

Evaluation drift. Separate input drift, concept drift, provider model drift and evaluator drift. Detect with windowed monitoring, PSI (below 0.1 stable, above 0.25 major, rule of thumb), fixed canary prompts, a frozen judge-calibration set and embedding/retrieval statistics. Pinned versions help but do not eliminate drift.

Upgrade risk. New models can break formats, style, instruction following, refusals, tool use, token counts, parameters and deprecation timelines. Pin ids, track retirement dates, run a per-slice paired regression suite, adapt prompts, shadow, canary, A/B, ramp, and keep a one-flag rollback.

Decision discipline. Write the decision rule first, report honestly when only cost or latency improved, keep a holdout and a changelog, and read raw outputs regularly.
